evidence: Cic. Off. 2.64: sed interdum etiam frūctuōsum
Mor. 28: interdum fessae succēdit laeva sorōrī
Caes. BG 1.8.4: nōn numquam interdiū, saepius noctū
Quint. 1.5.58: sīcut illī ā nōbīs nōnnumquam mūtuantur

terms.gloss: sometimes, now and then (as against never)
evidence: Sen. Ep. 83.6: aliquandō dormīsse mē sciō, aliquandō suspicor
Ter. Eun. 713: modo ait, modo negat
Liv. 1.5.5: rem inmātūram nisi per occāsiōnem aperīre nōluerat (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Traupman gives per occāsiōnem for “occasionally”; classically it means “on a favourable opportunity” (Lewis & Short). For “occasionally” use interdum or nōnnumquam.

phrases.latin: est enim nōn modo līberāle paulum nōn numquam dē suō jūre dēcēdere, sed interdum etiam frūctuōsum
phrases.english: for to give up a little of your rights now and then is not only generous but sometimes even profitable

phrases.latin: aliquandō dormīsse mē sciō, aliquandō suspicor
phrases.english: sometimes I know I’ve slept, sometimes I only suspect it
sometimes he says yes, sometimes no

aliquando.html: A compound of quandō, which de Vaan gives with a long final vowel (p. 507, s.v. quī); Festus records an older form quandōd (Lewis & Short s.v. quando). The Latinitas loci write aliquandō throughout, and the libellī quandō.

sources: Lewis & Short: interdum · Lewis & Short: nonnumquam · Lewis & Short: aliquando · Lewis & Short: modo
